# CPR and chest compressions
Examine the body and check its injuries, pulse and blood volume before resuscitation. Treat other lethal injuries and provide oxygen. Compressions do not replace missing blood or organs.
## Performing the procedure
Use the patient's context menu. Only one person can perform either procedure on a patient at a time. Stay in reach with a free hand and remove obstructing outer clothing. The first cycle takes 3 seconds; uninterrupted cycles then repeat every 0.8 seconds. Cancelling or changing the performer restarts the initial cycle.
Full CPR treats 3 suffocation damage per completed cycle and can provide an artificial breath. Both airways must be accessible, and the performer and patient need working lungs for artificial breathing. Chest compressions provide circulation and can restart a heart, but do not treat suffocation or provide artificial breaths. IPCs, people without functioning lungs and people whose physiology does not breathe can perform compressions. This does not make IPCs suitable CPR patients.
Both procedures support circulation after the first completed cycle, while the procedure continues. Existing blood loss still needs treatment. Compressions do not restart chemical metabolism in a dead body.
## Reviving a patient
CPR can revive a body while its examination still shows the green fresh-body message. Other lethal injuries and missing necessary organs must be treated first. The chance is checked after that cycle's treatment and depends on remaining suffocation damage. Its limit is half the patient's softcrit threshold: normally 50 for humans, or 60 for a body with a 120 threshold. At that limit or above the chance is zero; halfway to the limit it is 50%, and at zero suffocation it is 100% if the other requirements are met.
Successful CPR starts an installed stopped heart at its lowest stable pulse (normally 40 BPM), then the heart gradually recovers on its own. It does not correct an already beating but fibrillating heart. Use a defibrillator or appropriate medicine to treat that rhythm.
## After any revival
The patient spends 5 seconds in forced sleep, followed by 30 seconds of fading drowsiness. This recovery does not cause yawning or further random sleep incidents. Ongoing critical injuries or another cause of unconsciousness can keep the patient unconscious after those 5 seconds. Recheck the pulse and breathing and continue the appropriate treatment.
